\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{はかま} (hakama)}{はかま (hakama)}]{\ja{はかま} (hakama) — a hakama (pleated trousers)}

\label{lesson:JA-C105-hakama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a ball, then the Japanese for a bell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{はかま}}
\textbf{\ja{はかま}} — \emph{hakama} — \textquotedblleft{}a hakama (pleated trousers)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{はかま}} (\emph{hakama}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{ゆかた} (yukata)}{ゆかた (yukata)}]{\ja{ゆかた} (yukata) — a cotton kimono}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{ゆかた}} (\emph{yukata}) is a native word. JMdict writes it with characters for \textquotedblleft{}bathe\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}clothes\textquotedblright{}, read as a whole; it is usually explained as \emph{yu}, \textquotedblleft{}bath\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{katabira}, a light robe, shortened. That account is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}
